paras: The manhunt for Buford Monday was a search in August and September 1920 by armed posses across Madison, Jessamine and Fayette counties, Kentucky, for Buford Monday (also spelled Munday), a Black man accused of assaulting Mrs. Charles Sauers (also Sowers) of Valley View. Associated Press dispatches described several hundred farmers and county officers carrying guns, ropes and pitchforks, and one headline said he would be lynched if captured. No capture was reported, and the Chicago Whip, the one Black paper found to cover the case, said the alarm had been raised after Monday tipped his hat to the woman.

Monday was described as a light-skinned "mulatto" of about 28 who had lived for several years at Valley View, where he ran a lunch stand selling sandwiches and pies to train passengers. He had served in the army in France and was separated from his wife. Mrs. Sauers, 16, had married Charles Sauers, a farmer, the previous Christmas and was expecting a child.

According to the Lexington Herald, as reprinted in the Richmond Daily Register, Monday came to the Sowers home on the morning of Monday, August 2, asked whether she had chickens for sale and, on her refusal, knocked her down and threw a white powder in her face. Her husband found her on the floor hours later, and the AP reported that she regained consciousness only on the afternoon of August 4, when she said he had thrown "a powdered drug" in her face. The Richmond Daily Register instead placed the assault on Tuesday night and said she could not explain what had happened for more than four hours.

On Wednesday, August 4, a posse headed by Deputy Sheriff James Taylor of Valley View searched Madison and much of Fayette County, trailing Monday toward Lexington and then combing Richmond into the early morning. The posse called at the Richmond home of Sheriff Whitlock but "asked for no warrant" and had not notified the local authorities. AP dispatches put the searchers at several hundred farmers and county officers armed with guns or shotguns, ropes and pitchforks, and said Monday had been seen at Nicholasville. Lexington police and Fayette County deputies joined the search, and rumors placed him on trains toward Ashland or Lexington.

On August 5 the woman's brother, Herman Howard, filed a charge of criminal assault in the county court and said he feared that if Monday were captured "he would never reach jail." A week later he was reported near Burnside in Pulaski County, and Harry Hughes was sent from Nicholasville to investigate. On September 23 an armed posse of farmers searched near Hutchinson and Paris after another Black man said he had recognized Monday leaving a cornfield, and a second posse set out from Lexington, but neither found him.
No report of Monday's capture, trial or death appears in the coverage through late September 1920. Mrs. Sowers was reported recovering in mid-August and fully recovered by September 24.

The Associated Press story ran on August 5-7 in papers from Vermont to Oklahoma, including the Washington Evening Star and the Richmond Times-Dispatch. Its headlines stressed the weapons and the charge, such as "Armed With Guns Ropes and Pitchforks" and "Farmer Posse Hunts Negro," and the Guthrie Daily Leader declared that the "Brute" would "Be Lynched If Captured." In Kentucky the Mt. Sterling Advocate called Monday a "negro brute" and predicted that "quick justice" would follow his capture, while the Richmond Daily Register covered the hunt as local news, tracking the posse's movements and noting that it had bypassed the sheriff.

The Chicago Whip ran a short Lexington item on August 14 under the headline "Search With Guns for Polite Man." It said Monday had only tipped his hat to Mrs. Sauers, that she then "gave the alarm that he had attempted to assault her," and that police and citizens were hunting him with "engines of Southern warfare, bent upon lynching him on sight."

The accounts differ on the accusation itself: the white papers, drawing on the woman, her family and the posse, reported a completed assault with a drug or powder, while the Whip described a hat-tip turned into a charge of attempted assault and named no source. The papers also disagreed on whether it happened Monday or Tuesday and on the husband's first name.

reader.title: Manhunt for Buford Monday
bases: Armed posses of farmers and officers, carrying ropes, hunted an accused Black man whom papers said would be lynched if caught (A2, A5, A10, A17), but he was not caught, so this is a threatened lynching (manhunt) with no killing.

Posses of several hundred hunted Monday on an assault charge and papers predicted he would be lynched if captured (A2, A5, A10, A17), but no paper reports his capture or death through September (A18), so no one was killed.

The AP wire, the local Richmond Daily Register and the Mt. Sterling Advocate independently report the armed posse hunt (A1, A3, A4, A5), and the Chicago Whip confirms the hunt while disputing the accusation (A17).

accounts.label: Wire report (AP)
accounts.gist: Monday forcibly entered the Sauers home and assaulted the 16-year-old wife, throwing a powdered drug in her face; she was unconscious until Aug. 4; several hundred armed farmers and officers hunted him.

accounts.label: Local paper and Lexington Herald (accuser's family)
accounts.gist: He came asking to buy chickens, knocked her down and threw a white powder in her face; her brother filed the charge and feared a lynching.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Chicago Whip)
accounts.gist: Monday merely tipped his hat to Mrs. Sauers, who then alleged attempted assault, and the community was hunting him to lynch him on sight.

framing.detail: The Guthrie Daily Leader headlined the 'Brute' who 'Will Be Lynched If Captured' and the Mt. Sterling Advocate called him a 'negro brute' facing 'quick justice'.
The AP story ran widely under headlines stressing guns, ropes and pitchforks and the charge of assault on a white woman.
The Richmond Daily Register reported the hunt as a local crime story, noting the posse did not notify the sheriff, and called the charge an 'alleged assault' by late September.
The Chicago Whip's 'Search With Guns for Polite Man' presented the charge as an overreaction to a hat-tip and the hunt as 'Southern warfare'.

versions.value: Completed assault: forced entry, knocked her down, powdered drug or white powder thrown in her face, unconscious for hours
He tipped his hat to her and she alleged attempted assault

conflicts.note: The white version comes from the accuser, her family and the posse; the Whip's brief names no source. Neither is independent of a side.
The AP and the Lexington Herald agree on Monday (Aug. 2); the Richmond Daily Register twice says Tuesday.
Most reports, including the Register's later ones, say Charles.
The Register says she spoke to her husband before becoming unconscious, which may reconcile the two.
